questions.q: What does git merge create when combining two branches?
options: A new merge commit with two parents — the tip of each branch — preserving both histories exactly as they happened
A single branch with the other branch permanently deleted
No new commit at all
A copy of every file duplicated with new names
questions.explain: A merge commit has two parents, joining both branches' histories at that point without rewriting either one.

questions.q: What does git rebase actually do to your branch's commits?
options: It replays them one at a time on top of the target branch's current tip, creating new commits with new hashes
It deletes them permanently with no replacement
It leaves them completely unchanged and just relabels the branch
It automatically pushes them to the remote
questions.explain: Rebase rewrites your branch's commits as brand-new commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history — the originals are gone.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is it safe to rebase a branch?
options: When it's your own local feature branch that nobody else has pulled yet
Any time, on any branch, with no exceptions
Only after it has already been merged into main
Only when working with more than three collaborators
questions.explain: Rebasing rewrites history, so it's safe only when you're the sole owner of those commits — a local, unshared feature branch.

questions.q: Why should you never rebase a branch that's already shared or pushed?
options: A teammate who already pulled it will have history that disagrees with yours, forcing a confusing, avoidable mess
Git technically forbids rebasing any pushed branch and will error out
It will corrupt the remote repository permanently
Rebase only works on branches with fewer than two commits
questions.explain: Once a branch is shared, rewriting its history creates a mismatch between your rewritten commits and the ones teammates already have.

questions.q: What's the visible difference in git log --oneline --graph between a merged history and a rebased history?
options: Merge shows a merge commit joining two lines; rebase shows one clean, linear line with no merge commit
There is no visible difference between the two
Rebase always shows more commits than merge
Merge deletes the log entirely
questions.explain: Merge preserves the branching shape with a two-parent merge commit; rebase produces a single straight line since commits were replayed in sequence.
